title: Should voting be compulsory?

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: Turnout was fifty-two per cent. Somebody's going to propose compulsory voting again within the month.

turns.speaker: Amos
turns.text: Australia does it and gets into the nineties, so it plainly works at the thing it's aimed at.

turns.speaker: Piotr
turns.text: It works at attendance. Whether it works at democracy is a different question.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: Meaning uninformed people being made to choose.

turns.speaker: Piotr
turns.text: Meaning exactly that. A vote cast to avoid a fine isn't obviously worth more than a vote not cast.

turns.speaker: Amos
turns.text: Except who doesn't vote isn't random. It's the young, the poor and the recently moved, so low turnout systematically over-weights everyone else.

turns.speaker: Amos
turns.text: Parties then write manifestos for the people who show up, which makes the gap self-reinforcing.

turns.speaker: Piotr
turns.text: That's the strongest version of it, yes.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: The Australian detail I like is that it's compulsory attendance, not compulsory choice. You can spoil the ballot legally.

turns.speaker: Amos
turns.text: Which answers the freedom objection almost entirely.

turns.speaker: Piotr
turns.text: Almost. Being made to turn up is still compulsion even if you can hand in a blank paper.

turns.speaker: Jade
turns.text: There's a cheaper alternative nobody tries first, which is automatic registration. A good part of the gap is administrative rather than apathetic.

turns.speaker: Piotr
turns.text: That I'd support tomorrow, and it wouldn't need an argument about liberty at all.

points: Turnout of fifty-two per cent prompts discussion of compulsory voting.
Australia achieves over ninety per cent, showing it works at raising attendance.
Piotr objects that a vote cast to avoid a fine is not clearly worth more than abstention.
Amos's strongest argument is that non-voters are not a random group, so low turnout over-weights other voters and parties then write manifestos for those who show up.
Jade notes the Australian requirement is attendance rather than choice, since spoiling the ballot is legal, which largely answers the freedom objection.
Jade proposes automatic registration as a cheaper first step, since much of the gap is administrative, and Piotr agrees readily.
